313: Reading: at 800–900 K, A and B agree within 0.015, which is the size of the error from the interpolation functions and the short-range-order assumption. 314: CE+MC (icet version of route A, complete): ftphase.ce (icet enumeration → EAM relaxation → trainstation ARDR → mchammer SGC / VCSGC → solubility limits). The lattice CE trained on all 631 fcc orderings with 1–8 atoms has a CV error of 9.0–10.6 meV/atom regardless of the cutoffs (the limit set by the relaxation energy of the 13 % size mismatch). SGC MC on a lattice CE has no hysteresis (no strain barrier to nucleation), and the point just before the jump is a two-phase state of the 2,048 sites, so the branch integration + tangent of route B cannot be used. The dF/dx of VCSGC (κ = 200, 171 independent φ points in parallel, 284 s on mygardenx1) lies on the common tangent inside the gap but tilts by about 0.1 eV in a finite cell (interfacial free energy), so the solubility limit is read where the ideal dilute branch c + k_B T ln(x/(1−x)) fitted to the 4 end points reaches the two-phase level just inside the gap (solvus_from_vcsgc).
319: Reading: the CE+MC solubility limits hardly depend on temperature (Ag side 0.023 → 0.031), whereas direct MC gives 0.027 → 0.126 and A 0.042 → 0.078. The main cause is that the CE contains only static lattice energies and no vibrations (excess vibrational entropy, thermal expansion); Ag–Cu is known as a system where vibrations widen the solubility limits. The rest is the 9 meV/atom CE error (k_B T ln 2 ≈ 0.05 eV at 800 K corresponds to a factor of 2 in the solubility limit). Conclusion: dilute solubility limits are better done with B (direct MC) or A (ideal mixing + RK + vibrations); use CE+MC for systems where order–disorder, short-range order and defect interactions are essential (the B2 width of Ni–Al). To add vibrations to the CE, add the vibrational term of the 03A random cells separately as a function of x.
320: Verification of the melting points (two-phase coexistence MD, coexist.py, 6,144 atoms, 400 ps each, mygarden5): for pure Ag the solid grows at 1265 K and melts at 1290 K → T_m = 1265–1290 K. This agrees with the original authors' interface MC 1267 K; the TI route's 1320–1330 K is about 50 K too high. Cu is nearly stationary at 1325 K and melts at 1350 K → T_m = 1325–1350 K (original authors 1327 K, TI route +35 K).
321: Cause (calphy fe convergence test, pure Ag, 1275 K): G_solid − G_liquid is −5.9 meV/atom with 256 atoms and 10k switching steps, −4.6 with 256 atoms and 50k, +1.3 with 2,048 atoms and 10k, +0.5 with 2,048 atoms and 50k. The liquid is converged at 256 atoms, but the finite-size error of the solid Frenkel–Ladd, about 7 meV/atom too low at 256 atoms, is the origin of the +50 K melting point. The switching length is worth 1–2 meV. Remedy: use solid-TI cells of 2,000 atoms or more (solids_ti.min_atoms = 2000 is now the default). The Ni–Al solid TI (216–256 atoms) and the fcc Al TI of examples 3 and 4 carry the same error, and their melting points are 50–70 K too high.
